name: memset_benchmark (nadavrot): AVX2 assembly memset and memcpy for small sizes
baseline: glibc memset and memcpy (called directly and through the PLT), musl, and folly's memcpy
workload: Random-size memset and memcpy calls with buffer sizes 0 to 256 bytes (precomputed random sizes, nop-call overhead subtracted, trampoline prevents inlining); a second chart sweeps memset over sizes 0 to 512 bytes.
claimed_speedup: README: 'These implementations outperform the folly and glibc implementations.' Random-size chart values (docs/memset_r.png, docs/memcpy_r.png, lower is better, no unit printed): memset libc@plt 24344, libc 20172, asm_memset 14295; memcpy libc@plt 28285, libc 25263, folly 23969, asm_memcpy 21547. Ratios (derived from page data): memset about 1.41x faster than direct libc, memcpy about 1.17x faster than direct libc and 1.11x faster than folly. The size-sweep chart (docs/memset_bench.png, sizes 0 to 512) shows the new memset below direct glibc for roughly 32 to 224 bytes and 352 to 512 bytes, about level with it between 224 and 352 bytes and under 32 bytes, and musl is slower than the new memset for most sizes.
compiler_and_flags: CMakeLists.txt sets -O3 -g3 -march=native -Wall (default build type RelWithDebInfo); compiler name and version, and the glibc version, are not stated.
stars_or_usage: 344 stars; memset landed in facebook/folly as folly/memset.S (Apache-2.0, Copyright Facebook)
tradeoffs: x86-64 only (System V ABI assembly in src/memset/impl.S and src/memcpy/impl.S; memset uses AVX2 vmovdqu/vpbroadcastb), built with -march=native, so the benchmark numbers are for one unnamed microarchitecture and the code needs AVX2. Tuned for the 0 to 256 byte range (size distribution measured from Chrome), not for large copies. No LICENSE file in the repository, so the code is reference only; the folly copy of memset is Apache-2.0 and is the copyable route. Ships exhaustive correctness tests and LD_PRELOAD proxy and histogram tools.
caveats: First-party charts only: the README gives no numbers in text, no CPU model and no compiler or glibc version, and the chart axes have no unit. glibc was tested as it shipped, so it dispatches to its own AVX or ERMS variants; the size-sweep chart shows the new code is not faster across the whole 0 to 512 range (about equal to glibc between roughly 224 and 352 bytes). Commits end in January 2022. The link to the Hacker News thread 'A 100LOC C impl of memset, that is faster than glibc's' is inferred from title and date (thread not opened), so treat the HN connection as probable, not confirmed.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch (news.ycombinator.com) 'Show HN memcpy strlen memchr assembly faster than glibc' returned the thread 'A 100LOC C impl of memset, that is faster than glibc's' (item 29197161); thread could not be opened (news.ycombinator.com DNS blocked), so the repo was matched by title and date, then opened on github.com.

name: memchr (BurntSushi): SIMD memchr, memrchr and memmem for Rust
baseline: libc memmem and libc memchr (host libc through the rebar 'libc' engine; libc name and version not recorded)
workload: rebar benchmark suite: 54 substring-search benchmarks (English, Russian and Chinese subtitles, Sherlock text, Rust source code, pathological inputs) and 15 single-byte memchr benchmarks over short and huge haystacks, one-shot API (searcher built per call) so libc is comparable.
claimed_speedup: Recorded run benchmarks/record/x86_64/2026-07-30.csv, rebar speed ratio (1.00 is best on every benchmark, lower is better), geometric mean (derived from page data): memmem one-shot over 54 benchmarks libc memmem 2.25 versus memchr crate 1.11; the crate is faster on 37 of 54, libc faster on 17, per-benchmark ratio range 0.32 to 40.7. Single-byte memchr one-shot over 15 benchmarks libc 1.13 versus crate 1.03; libc is faster on 2 huge-haystack cases (about 0.8x of the crate time) and the crate is faster or equal on 13. README separately reports, for the 2023-08-26 record against Rust std: prebuilt memmem 1.03 versus std 6.50, one-shot 1.04 versus std 5.26.
compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release for both the crate engine and the libc engine (engines/libc calls libc::memchr and libc::memmem through the libc crate); rustc and libc versions are not recorded in the CSV (engine version for libc is 'unknown').
hardware: x86_64 record; CPU model not stated in the CSV or the benchmarks directory.
stars_or_usage: 1.6k stars; the 'memchr' crate is a dependency of ripgrep and the Rust regex engine
tradeoffs: Rust only: no C or C++ API ships with the crate (usable from C++ only through a hand-written FFI wrapper; the C ABI repo memx-cdy wraps a different crate). Runtime AVX2 dispatch needs the std feature; SSE2, wasm32 and aarch64 SIMD paths exist, other targets fall back to SWAR. Prebuilt Finder objects amortize searcher construction, which C memmem cannot do. Pathological inputs are guarded by Two-Way fallback, so worst case is linear.
caveats: The suite (rebar) is written by the crate author, and the CPU model and libc version behind the recorded CSV are not given, so this stays first-party tier C. Ratios in claimed_speedup were computed from the committed CSV, not quoted from a README: the README's own comparison is against Rust std, not libc. The libc engine measures FFI calls to the host libc, and libc memmem is often faster on a few cases (for example Rust library code with the needle 'common-paren' and pathological rare-repeated matches). Found through HN discussion of memmem benchmarks where a commenter quoted rebar geometric means of 1.07 (crate) versus 3.15 (glibc memmem, one-shot), a snippet that could not be opened and that differs from the 2026 record.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch (news.ycombinator.com) 'Show HN memchr memmem strstr SIMD AVX2 library faster than memchr glibc' returned the threads 'SIMD-friendly algorithms for substring searching (2016)' and 'Show HN: StringZilla v3...' whose comments cite the memchr crate; repo and CSV opened on github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com.

name: Apex memmove (Trevor Herselman): SSE2 memcpy and memmove for x86 and x64
baseline: C library memcpy and memmove (the README names no baseline; the repo's source has no comparison)
workload: No benchmark in the repository. README only says 'The fastest memcpy/memmove on x86/x64 ... EVER, written in C (according to the author)' and links the original CodeProject article, which could not be opened.
claimed_speedup: No numbers on the pages opened ('fastest memcpy/memmove on x86/x64 ... EVER').
stars_or_usage: 14 stars; the code is by Trevor Herselman (written 2014), mirrored by rukkal; discussed on Hacker News as 'Apex memmove' and in an Ultimate++ forum thread
tradeoffs: x86 and x86-64 only (SSE2 intrinsics from emmintrin.h, cpuid dispatch via __cpuid or __get_cpuid, several variants named tiberium, kryptonite and mithril); falls back to the library functions elsewhere. No license text anywhere in the repository or file headers, so the code is reference only. Handles overlapping moves like memmove.
caveats: Tier D: only a self-description with no numbers in the repository. Search-result snippets of third-party posts mention a single-machine MSVC test (about 3.55 ms versus 4.37 ms for the CRT memcpy) but those pages could not be opened, so none of it is claimed here. The mirror has three commits, all dated 2016-09-22, and no tests or benchmark code, so the claim cannot be reproduced from the repository. Targets 2014-era CPUs, long before ERMS and FSRM made rep movsb competitive in glibc.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch (news.ycombinator.com) 'Show HN memcpy strlen memchr assembly faster than glibc' returned the thread 'Apex memmove' (item 12047981); thread could not be opened, repo and raw source opened on github.com.
